prompt: Writes no longer fit on one primary. Why does adding secondaries to the replica set not help?

choices.text: Each secondary is another full copy that still follows the one primary
choices.why: Right. A replica set multiplies safety, not capacity.

choices.text: Secondaries refuse writes until they are promoted by hand
choices.why: They refuse client writes by design, and promotion is an election, not a manual step.

choices.text: A replica set is limited to three members
choices.why: It allows more; the limit is that every member stores and applies everything.

choices.text: Secondaries slow the primary down by asking for the oplog too often
choices.why: Fetching the oplog is cheap; the problem is that all writes still go to one machine.

prompt: Match each server of a sharded cluster to what it does.
hint: One description belongs to none of them.

pairs.right: routes each request to the shards that hold the data
keeps the map of which range lives on which shard
stores its part of each sharded collection

right_distractors: elects the primary of every replica set

prompt: Before sharding a collection that is slow, what does the lesson say to try first?

choices.text: Indexes, a bigger machine, archiving old data or secondary reads
choices.why: Right. Each costs less and is undone in an afternoon; a shard key is not.

choices.text: A hashed shard key, since it is the safe default for any collection
choices.why: Hashed keys scatter range queries; there is no key that is safe by default.

choices.text: A second mongos, so the router stops being the bottleneck
choices.why: Without sharding there is no router at all.

choices.text: Nothing: shard as early as possible, while the collection is small
choices.why: Sharding is the last thing to reach for, because the key is expensive to change.

prompt: In `cluster.sh`, why is each shard started as a replica set even though it has a single member?

choices.text: Because a single-member set starts faster than a standalone server would
choices.why: Speed is not the reason; the cluster requires the form.

choices.text: Because in a sharded cluster shards and config servers are replica sets
choices.why: Right. One member keeps the lab small; production gives each set three.

choices.text: So that `mongos` can read from secondaries
choices.why: With one member there are no secondaries.

choices.text: So that `--wiredTigerCacheSizeGB` takes effect
choices.why: The cache setting works on any mongod.

prompt: What does `mongos` store?

choices.text: A copy of the config server's map, written to its own disk
choices.why: It reads the map from the config server; it keeps nothing durable.

choices.text: Recent query results, as a cache
choices.why: It routes; it does not cache documents.

choices.text: Nothing
choices.why: Right. That is why the script gives it no data directory and no replica set.

choices.text: The documents of unsharded collections
choices.why: Those live on the database's primary shard.

prompt: Why does every `mongod` in `cluster.sh` get `--wiredTigerCacheSizeGB 0.25`?

choices.text: So that the data files are compressed
choices.why: Compression is a separate setting; this one is memory.

choices.text: Otherwise each would size its cache from the whole machine's memory
choices.why: Right, and three of them would compete for the same memory.

choices.text: Because a shard refuses to start with more than a gigabyte of cache
choices.why: There is no such refusal; the default is just too large for a shared VM.

choices.text: So that the balancer moves ranges in smaller pieces
choices.why: Range size is set per collection with `configureCollectionBalancing`.

prompt: Each shard owned 5,000 orders after the first 10,000. After orders 10,001 to 20,000 were inserted under the ranged key, how many did `shard2` own?
Why does splitting the top range again not fix a growing shard key?

choices.text: The newest piece is still on one shard, and every new value lands in it
choices.why: Right. The hot spot moves with the top of the range.

choices.text: Splitting is refused for a key with consecutive values
choices.why: Splits work; they just do not change where new values go.

choices.text: The balancer moves the split pieces back together again
choices.why: The balancer moves ranges between shards; it does not undo splits to punish them.

choices.text: A split deletes the documents already in the range
choices.why: A split only changes the map.

prompt: Under a hashed `orderId`, which query is sent to every shard?
hint: What does a hash do to neighbouring values?

choices.text: `find({ orderId: 12345 })`
choices.why: An exact value hashes to one place: `SINGLE_SHARD`.

choices.text: `find({ orderId: { $gte: 100, $lt: 200 } })`
choices.why: Right: `SHARD_MERGE`. The hundred neighbouring numbers were scattered on purpose.

choices.text: Neither: a hashed key makes every query single-shard
choices.why: The capture showed the range query as `SHARD_MERGE`.

choices.text: Both, since hashing hides which shard owns a value
choices.why: `mongos` hashes the exact value itself and knows where it lives.

prompt: A query on `orders` filters by `customer`, a field that is not in the shard key. How many shards does `mongos` ask?

choices.text: Only the shard that holds most of that customer's orders
choices.why: `mongos` has no way to know that; the map is by shard key.

choices.text: One, chosen at random
choices.why: A random shard would miss the orders on the others.

choices.text: All of them, whatever the key's kind
choices.why: Right: `SHARD_MERGE`, under the ranged and the hashed key alike.

choices.text: The primary shard of the database
choices.why: A sharded collection is spread over every shard, not kept on the primary one.

prompt: In `explain()` through `mongos`, the top stage `___` means the query went to exactly one shard.
hint: Two words joined by an underscore.

prompt: Ninety seconds after the inserts, `shard1` showed 66,538 owned visits and 33,462 orphaned. What are the orphaned ones?

choices.text: Visits whose insert failed and was never acknowledged
choices.why: Every insert was acknowledged; the count came back as 100,000.

choices.text: Copies left behind by migrations, deleted after a delay
choices.why: Right. The ranges now belong to `shard2`, and counts through `mongos` leave the old copies out.

choices.text: Visits with no `country` field, which no range can hold
choices.why: Every visit had `"BR"`.

choices.text: Duplicates that will be counted twice until the balancer finishes
choices.why: `mongos` already excludes them from counts.

prompt: A collection is sharded on `{ status: 1 }`, where status is one of four words. Ten shards are added. How many can ever hold its data?
hint: A range can only be cut between two different values.

choices.text: All ten, once the balancer has run long enough
choices.why: No amount of balancing splits a range holding a single value.

choices.text: At most four
choices.why: Right. Cardinality is a ceiling on how far the collection can spread.

choices.text: Exactly two, since the balancer works in pairs of shards
choices.why: It moves between pairs at a time, but it uses every shard over time.

choices.text: One, because a string key cannot be split
choices.why: Strings split fine between different values.

prompt: Why did the lesson set the range size of its collections to 1 MB?

choices.text: At the 128 MB default a lab collection is too small for the balancer to act
choices.why: Right. It acts only when the gap passes about three range sizes.

choices.text: Because ranges larger than 1 MB are marked jumbo
choices.why: Jumbo means indivisible, not large.

choices.text: To make `getShardDistribution` print smaller numbers
choices.why: The setting changes behaviour, not how numbers print.

choices.text: Because MongoDB 8.0 requires it for compound keys
choices.why: No such requirement; `orders` used the default.

prompt: What did `sh.splitFind` answer for the collection keyed on `{ country: 1 }`?

choices.text: That the range was split into two
choices.why: It could not be.

choices.text: `CannotSplit`: the chunk is indivisible
choices.why: Right. Every document had the same key value.

choices.text: That the balancer was disabled for this collection
choices.why: It was enabled throughout; it had marked the range jumbo.

choices.text: That `country` needed an index first
choices.why: Sharding creates the key's index; the problem was the single value.

prompt: Which change can `refineCollectionShardKey` make?

choices.text: Replace the first field of the key
choices.why: The new key must start with the old one.

choices.text: Turn a ranged key into a hashed one
choices.why: That needs `reshardCollection`, as the lesson did for `orders`.

choices.text: Add fields to the end of the existing key
choices.why: Right, and nothing moves when it does.

choices.text: Remove a field that the queries no longer use at all
choices.why: Refining only appends.

prompt: `reshardCollection` on 20,000 orders took 332.94 seconds. To the nearest whole minute, how long was that?
Why did resharding 20,000 small orders take over five minutes?

choices.text: By default it copies for at least five minutes, to let the shards catch up with writes
choices.why: Right. On a real collection the copy itself then dominates.

choices.text: Because the lab's shards are single members and copy slowly
choices.why: Copying 20,000 small documents takes well under a second here.

choices.text: Because a hashed key has to be computed for every document twice over
choices.why: Hashing is cheap; the time is a deliberate minimum.

choices.text: Because writes were blocked for the whole operation
choices.why: Writes are blocked only for a short moment at the switch-over.

prompt: A team plans to reshard because one shard is overloaded. What should they check first?

choices.text: That the new key starts with the old one
choices.why: That is refining's rule; resharding takes any key.

choices.text: Free disk for a second copy, and load headroom on an already struggling cluster
choices.why: Right. Resharding moves the whole collection through the shards it is meant to relieve.

choices.text: That the balancer is disabled for good
choices.why: Nothing in the lesson asks for that.

choices.text: That `mongos` is restarted after the change
choices.why: The router reads the new map on its own.

prompt: Put the building of the lab's cluster in order, as `cluster.sh` does it.
items: Start the config server and the two shards
Initiate a one-member replica set on each
Start `mongos`, pointing it at the config server
trap: `mongos` reads the map from a config server that has to be running and initiated.

prompt: Which of these are true of the lab's cluster? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: A hashed `orderId` spread 20,000 consecutive orders almost evenly
A key with a single value was split once the balancer had time
choices.why: It stayed one jumbo range until the key was refined.

choices.text: Refining the key let the balancer move ranges it could not move before
choices.why: Right: three ranges went to `shard2`.

choices.text: Resharding left the range query on `orders` single-shard
choices.why: Under the new hashed key it became `SHARD_MERGE`.

prompt: A shop's queries mostly ask for one customer's orders, newest first. Which shard key fits best?

choices.text: `{ orderId: 1, customer: 1, placedAt: -1 }`
choices.why: A key that starts with a growing value puts every new order on one shard, and the query does not lead with it.

choices.text: `{ customer: 1, placedAt: -1 }`
choices.why: Right. Writes spread over customers, and one customer's history sits on one shard.

choices.text: `{ status: 1 }`
choices.why: Low cardinality: a handful of values can never spread far.

choices.text: `{ placedAt: "hashed" }`
choices.why: Writes spread, but every customer query asks every shard.
